generic: Write as a native speaker would for a modern consumer app: natural, idiomatic, never calqued. Register: use the informal address if modern youth-oriented app copy in this language uses it, but keep the polite/formal form if this language stays formal in app copy regardless of audience age — get the modern feel from fresh, light phrasing, not forced slang.

locales.ar: Modern Standard Arabic (MSA), not a regional dialect. MSA has no polite/casual pronoun split: address the reader with the standard second-person singular (generic masculine), as Apple's Arabic UI and mainstream apps do, and get a warm, contemporary feel through fresh, light phrasing. Right-to-left: keep punctuation and any Latin tokens (e.g. "iCloud") correctly placed for RTL.
locales.bn: Conversational Bengali (Bangla) in Bengali script. Keep the polite "আপনি" — Apple's Bengali UI and mainstream Bengali apps address readers of every age politely; the casual "তুমি"/"তুই" from an app reads as overfamiliar. The modern feel comes from warmth, brevity, and natural English loanwords (e.g. "budget"), not informal pronouns.
locales.ca: Use the informal "tu", not "vostè" — the everyday address in Apple's Catalan UI and mainstream Catalan apps, natural for readers of every age. Natural, friendly Catalan as used in Apple's Catalan UI; warmth comes from clear, unfussy phrasing, not slang.
locales.cs: Use the polite "vy" (vykání: second-person plural verb forms, lowercase "vy/váš"), the respectful norm in Apple's Czech UI and mainstream Czech apps and banks; "ty" still reads overfamiliar to many readers. Warmth comes from modern, natural phrasing over literal calques, not from tykání; avoid stiff officialese.
locales.da: Use the informal "du" — the universal address in Danish apps, Apple's included, for readers of every age ("De" reads archaic). Direct and plain.
locales.de: Use the informal "du" — Apple's German UI and most mainstream German apps, finance apps like N26 and Trade Republic included, now address readers of every age with "du". Keep it respectful: warm and direct, never chummy or slangy; avoid stiff officialese and English calques. German typically runs longer than English — keep compounds tight so labels don't overflow.
locales.el: Use the polite plural "εσείς" (plural verb forms and "σας") — the respectful norm in Apple's Greek UI and mainstream Greek apps and banks; the singular "εσύ" reads overfamiliar to older readers. Warmth comes from modern, everyday Greek; avoid overly formal or bureaucratic phrasing.
locales.en-AU: Australian English spelling and idiom (e.g. "organise", "colour"). Relaxed, friendly tone.
locales.es: Castilian Spanish; use the informal "tú", not "usted" (and not "vosotros" for a single reader). Apple Spain and mainstream Spanish apps and banks address readers of every age with "tú". Spain vocabulary (e.g. "móvil"). Modern and relaxed, never slangy.
locales.es-MX: Latin American Spanish; use the informal "tú", not "usted" — Apple's Latin American UI and mainstream apps, banking included, use it with readers of every age; keep it courteous, never slangy. Neutral LatAm vocabulary (e.g. "celular"); avoid Spain-specific terms.
locales.fi: Use the informal second-person singular (sinä forms, mostly implicit in the verb, e.g. "Lisää") — the universal address in Finnish apps, Apple's included, for readers of every age; the plural "te" reads stiff. Direct, natural Finnish app tone, not literal. Finnish runs long — keep UI labels tight.
locales.fr: Use the polite "vous" — Apple's French UI and mainstream French apps (banks, retail, transport) address readers with "vous", and "tu" from an app still reads presumptuous to many. Warmth comes from clear, light, unfussy phrasing, never stiff administrative French. Elegant and concise; prefer natural French terms over anglicisms. French app copy prizes clarté and a refined, slightly understated register over an enthusiastic one.
locales.fr-CA: Canadian French; use the polite "vous" — Apple's Canadian French UI and mainstream Québec banking and public-service apps keep "vous" even though "tu" is common in speech. Warmth comes from plain, friendly phrasing, not tutoiement. Prefer Québécois usage and OQLF-style avoidance of anglicisms where they differ from France French.
locales.gu: Conversational Gujarati in Gujarati script. Keep the polite "તમે" — Apple's Gujarati UI and mainstream Gujarati apps address readers of every age politely; the casual "તું" reads as overfamiliar. The modern feel comes from warmth, brevity, and natural English loanwords (e.g. "budget"), not informal pronouns.
locales.he: Modern Hebrew, with no polite/casual pronoun split; the real choice is gender — avoid gendered second-person forms: use infinitives for actions (e.g. "להוסיף") and noun phrases for labels, and where direct address is unavoidable use plural imperatives (e.g. "הוסיפו"), never slash forms, as Apple's Hebrew UI and mainstream Israeli apps do for readers of every age. Right-to-left: keep punctuation and any Latin tokens (e.g. "iCloud") correctly placed for RTL. Friendly register; warmth comes from clear, natural phrasing.
locales.hi: Conversational Hindi in Devanagari. Keep the polite "आप": Apple's Hindi UI and mainstream Hindi apps use "आप" for readers of every age; "तू" would read as rude. The modern feel comes from warmth, brevity, and natural English loanwords (e.g. "budget"), not informal pronouns.
locales.hr: Use the polite "vi" (second-person plural verb forms, lowercase "vi/vaš") — the respectful norm in Apple's Croatian UI and mainstream Croatian apps and banks; "ti" reads overfamiliar to older readers. Warmth comes from modern, natural phrasing, not calqued and not informal.
locales.hu: Use polite address (magázás) through formal third-person verb forms (e.g. "Adja meg", "költségvetése"), using "Ön" only when a pronoun is unavoidable and never "maga" — the respectful norm in Apple's Hungarian UI and mainstream banks; tegezés still reads overfamiliar to older readers. Warmth comes from modern, plain phrasing, never stiff or bureaucratic register. Hungarian runs long — keep labels tight.
locales.id: Use the polite "Anda" — the standard written address in Apple's Indonesian UI, banks and official copy, respectful to readers of every age; the casual "kamu" can read overfamiliar to older readers. Warmth comes from friendly, plain everyday Indonesian as used in popular consumer apps, not slang.
locales.it: Use the informal "tu" — Apple's Italian UI and mainstream Italian apps and banks address readers of every age with "tu"; "Lei" reads stiff. Natural, courteous Italian, never slangy; avoid unnecessary anglicisms.
locales.ja: Keep polite-friendly です/ます — Apple's Japanese UI and mainstream Japanese apps stay polite for readers of every age; plain/casual form from an app reads as off. Get warmth through light, soft, approachable phrasing (Apple Japan's voice), not by dropping politeness; avoid stiff keigo. Use katakana for loanwords (e.g. アプリ). The English em-dash habit does not translate — restructure instead.
locales.kn: Natural Kannada in Kannada script. Keep the polite "ನೀವು" — the respectful norm in Apple's Kannada UI and mainstream Kannada apps, natural for readers of every age; the casual "ನೀನು" reads as overfamiliar. The modern feel comes from warmth, brevity, and natural English loanwords (e.g. "budget"), not informal pronouns.
locales.ko: Use the polite-friendly 해요체 throughout. Apple Korea and mainstream Korean apps stay polite with readers of every age; plain 반말 reads as wrong, and the stiffer 합니다체 reads distant, so don't drift into it (short button labels can stay noun forms). Warmth comes from clean, light phrasing and natural English loanwords (common in Korean tech), not from dropping politeness. Match Apple Korea's voice.
locales.ml: Natural Malayalam in Malayalam script. Keep the polite "നിങ്ങൾ" — Malayalam app copy addresses all audiences politely; the casual "നീ" reads as overfamiliar. The modern feel comes from warmth, brevity, and natural English loanwords (e.g. "budget"), not informal pronouns.
locales.mr: Conversational Marathi in Devanagari. Keep the polite "तुम्ही" — Marathi app copy stays polite for readers of every age; "तू" reads as overfamiliar. The modern feel comes from warmth, brevity, and natural English loanwords (e.g. "budget"), not informal pronouns.
locales.ms: Use the polite, neutral "anda" — the standard address in Apple's Malay UI and mainstream Malaysian apps and banks for readers of every age; casual "awak"/"kau" read overfamiliar. Warmth comes from friendly, natural Malay as used in consumer apps, not slang.
locales.nb: Norwegian (Bokmål); use the informal "du" — the universal address in Norwegian apps, Apple's included, for readers of every age ("De" reads archaic). Direct and plain.
locales.nl: Use the informal "je" — Apple's Dutch UI and mainstream Dutch apps and banks address readers of every age with "je"; "u" reads distant. Modern, relaxed, courteous register.
locales.or: Natural Odia in Odia script. Keep the polite "ଆପଣ" — the respectful norm in Apple's Odia UI and mainstream Odia apps, natural for readers of every age; the casual "ତୁମେ"/"ତୁ" reads as overfamiliar. The modern feel comes from warmth, brevity, and natural English loanwords (e.g. "budget"), not informal pronouns.
locales.pa: Conversational Punjabi in Gurmukhi (Indian Punjabi) script. Keep the polite "ਤੁਸੀਂ": Apple's Punjabi UI and mainstream Punjabi apps stay polite with readers of every age; "ਤੂੰ" reads as overfamiliar. The modern feel comes from warmth, brevity, and natural English loanwords (e.g. "budget"), not informal pronouns.
locales.pl: Use the informal second-person singular (imperatives like "Dodaj", and the courtesy capital "Twój/Twoja" when a possessive is needed) — the standard address in Polish software, Apple's included, and mainstream banking apps, for readers of every age; "Pan/Pani" is clumsy in UI. Friendly, natural, not stiff.
locales.pt-BR: Brazilian Portuguese; use "você" — Brazil's natural, respectful everyday address, used by Apple and mainstream apps for readers of every age ("o senhor/a senhora" is ceremonious, "tu" regional). Warm, not slangy. Brazilian orthography and vocabulary.
locales.pt-PT: European Portuguese; use polite third-person address — third-person verbs with "o seu/a sua", leaving the pronoun "você" out (it can read curt) — as Apple Portugal and mainstream Portuguese banks and retailers do; "tu" reads overfamiliar to older readers. Warmth comes from light, direct phrasing, not tutear. European orthography and vocabulary; avoid Brazilian-specific terms.
locales.ro: Modern Romanian; use the polite second-person plural (dumneavoastră verb forms, e.g. "Adăugați"; write the pronoun out, not "dvs.", and only when unavoidable) — the respectful norm in Apple's Romanian UI and mainstream Romanian apps and banks; "tu" reads overfamiliar. Warmth comes from modern, natural phrasing, not informality.
locales.ru: Use the polite "вы" (lowercase, as in UI copy) — Apple's Russian UI and mainstream Russian apps and banks address readers with "вы"; "ты" from an app reads overfamiliar. Warmth comes from natural, light, non-calque Russian, not bureaucratic канцелярит.
locales.sk: Use the polite "vy" (vykanie: second-person plural verb forms, lowercase "vy/váš") consistently, never mixing in tykanie — the respectful norm in Apple's Slovak UI and mainstream Slovak apps and banks, for readers of every age. Modern Slovak; warmth comes from natural phrasing, not informality.
locales.sl: Use the polite "vi" (vikanje: second-person plural verb forms, lowercase), the respectful norm in Apple's Slovenian UI and mainstream Slovenian apps and banks; "ti" reads overfamiliar to many readers. Warmth comes from natural, non-calqued phrasing, not tikanje. Note Slovenian's dual number: count-dependent strings need the dual ("two") form, not just one/other.
locales.sv: Use the informal "du" — the universal address in Swedish apps, Apple's included, for readers of every age ("ni" reads stiff). Direct and plain.
locales.ta: Natural Tamil in Tamil script. Keep the polite "நீங்கள்" — Tamil app copy stays polite for readers of every age; the casual "நீ" reads as overfamiliar. The modern feel comes from warmth, brevity, and natural English loanwords (e.g. "budget"), not informal pronouns.
locales.te: Natural Telugu in Telugu script. Keep the polite "మీరు" — Apple's Telugu UI and mainstream Telugu apps and banks stay polite for readers of every age; the casual "నువ్వు" reads as overfamiliar. The modern feel comes from warmth, brevity, and natural English loanwords (e.g. "budget"), not informal pronouns.
locales.th: Polite, friendly Thai — address the reader as "คุณ" or leave the pronoun out, as Apple's Thai UI and mainstream apps do, and get politeness from polite phrasing (e.g. โปรด/กรุณา where natural), not from the speaker-gendered particles ครับ/ค่ะ, which UI strings don't use; the modern feel comes from light, contemporary phrasing, not from dropping politeness. Follow normal Thai spacing conventions.
locales.tr: Use the polite "siz" (plural verb forms and suffixes, e.g. "Ekleyin", "bütçeniz"); short button labels may use the bare stem ("Ekle", "Sil") as Turkish UI normally does. Apple's Turkish UI and mainstream Turkish banks address readers with "siz"; "sen" reads overfamiliar. Warmth comes from friendly, natural phrasing, not from "sen".
locales.uk: Use the polite "ви" (lowercase, as in UI copy) — the respectful norm in Apple's Ukrainian UI and most mainstream Ukrainian apps and services, natural for readers of every age; "ти" reads overfamiliar. Warmth comes from modern, natural phrasing, not calqued from Russian or English.
locales.ur: Conversational Urdu in Nastaliq (Arabic) script. Keep the polite "آپ": Apple's Urdu UI and mainstream Urdu apps use "آپ" for readers of every age; "تم"/"تو" reads as overfamiliar or rude. Right-to-left: keep punctuation and any Latin tokens (e.g. "iCloud") correctly placed for RTL. The modern feel comes from warm, light phrasing and natural English loanwords (e.g. "budget"), not informal pronouns.
locales.vi: Address the reader as "bạn", or leave the pronoun out — the neutral, respectful address of Apple's Vietnamese UI and mainstream Vietnamese apps for readers of every age; never casual pronouns like "cậu"/"mày", and not the service-counter "quý khách". Friendly, natural Vietnamese as used in popular consumer apps.
locales.zh-Hans: Simplified Chinese, mainland China conventions. Address the reader as "你" consistently, as Apple's mainland UI and mainstream apps do for readers of every age; "您" reads like a bank or customer-service script. Concise, modern app tone; avoid Taiwan-specific vocabulary. Mainland copy is punchy and benefit-dense — short rhythms land well, but keep it calm and avoid exclamation-heavy hype.
locales.zh-Hant: Traditional Chinese, Taiwan conventions. Address the reader as "你" consistently, as Apple Taiwan's UI does for readers of every age; don't drift into "您" (e.g. in error or sync messages), which reads like a bank or customer-service script. Concise, modern app tone; avoid mainland-specific vocabulary.
